Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Name the three components of the Female Athlete Triad.
Understand the Female Athlete Triad as a spectrum of disease.
Understand how low energy availability occurs and how it affects menstrual function and bone
health.
Recognize high-risk sports, behaviors, and injuries that should prompt additional evaluation.
Perform appropriate screening for the Female Athlete Triad.
Understand that athletes with low energy availability can have a normal body mass index and
stable weight.
Recognize that moderate- and high-risk athletes are best evaluated and cared for by a
multidisciplinary team that can address the physical, psychologic, and nutritional needs of
these patients.
Understand that functional hypothalamic amenorrhea is a diagnosis of exclusion.

Identify which athletes should have their bone mineral density evaluated via a dual-energy x-
ray absorptiometry scan.
Understand that management should center on increased energy availability via increased
caloric intake and potentially decreased training volume and that pharmacologic treatment
should only be considered in patients in whom nonpharmacologic treatment fails.
Understand that medical clearance for sport in athletes with the Female Athlete Triad is
complex and should be performed by a multidisciplinary team experienced in the care of
these athletes.
Background
The Female Athlete Triad (the Triad) is a group of interrelated medical conditions observed in
physically active females. The Triad has three components:
Low energy availability with or without disordered eating
Menstrual dysfunction
Low BMD
Low energy availability causes menstrual dysfunction, including amenorrhea and
oligomenorrhea.
Menstrual dysfunction and low energy availability independently negatively affect bone health,
putting athletes at risk for osteoporosis and injury if not corrected.
The Triad is a spectrum of disease. At the healthy end of the spectrum, energy availability is
equal to or above the sum of energy expenditure and resting metabolic demands.
At the opposite end of the continuum are the clinical endpoints of the syndrome: low energy
availability with or without disordered eating, functional hypothalamic amenorrhea (FHA), and
osteoporosis.
Early recognition and management may prevent progression to the clinical endpoints and
long-lasting difficulties with osteoporosis and reproductive function.

Background
The Triad is a group of interrelated medical conditions that occur in physically active
females, from recreationally exercising girls and women to competitors at the highest
level. The American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM) first brought attention to the
Triad in 1992, and the ACSM published the first position statement addressing the Triad
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:07 PM
AAOS | Female Athlete Triad
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002089
2/29

in 1997. The statement described the Triad as a clinical syndrome that includes three
distinct but interrelated issues: disordered eating, osteoporosis, and amenorrhea.1
Disordered eating reduces the amount of energy available for physiologic functions and
may lead to amenorrhea and osteoporosis via homeostatic mechanisms of conserving
energy.
After the publication of the 1997 position statement, research identified negative
consequences with subclinical presentations that did not meet the original diagnostic
guidelines for the Triad. Low energy availability, even in the absence of disordered
eating, was found to be enough to suppress metabolic and reproductive hormones,
increase bone resorption, and suppress bone formation.2,3 In addition, athletes with
oligomenorrhea or subclinical menstrual dysfunction, such as anovulatory cycles, who
had not progressed to amenorrhea were found to have mild to moderately low BMD and
an increased incidence of stress fractures.4,5 Therefore, the definition was modified in
the 2007 ACSM position stand to include low energy availability with or without
disordered eating, menstrual dysfunction, and low BMD.6
This change placed emphasis on the Triad as a spectrum of disease, with the goal of
identifying athletes before the clinical endpoints of amenorrhea and osteoporosis,
present in the original definition, were reached. The Triad is now understood to be a
continuum. If health is optimized, energy availability meets energy expenditure,
including resting metabolic demands and energy expenditure via physical activity. At the
far opposite end of the continuum are the clinical endpoints of the syndrome: low
energy availability with or without disordered eating, FHA, and osteoporosis.7 Early
recognition and management can prevent progression to the clinical endpoints and
long-lasting consequences of osteoporosis and reproductive dysfunction.
Epidemiology and Risk Factors
The exact prevalence of the Triad is unknown, but athletes of all skill levels are known to be
affected.
A small percentage of female athletes (zero to 15.9%) have been shown to exhibit all three
Triad components. Up to 60% of competitive female athletes may exhibit one of the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:07 PM
AAOS | Female Athlete Triad
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002089
3/29

components.
The incidence is generally higher in certain sports, such as gymnastics, swimming, dance, and
distance running.
Behaviors with greatest risk for low energy availability include:
Limiting caloric intake
Following restrictive diets, such as veganism or vegetarianism
Specializing in a single sport early in life
Dieting for sport
Highest risk periods of time include:
Injury
Traumatic events or periods of worsened mental health
Rapidly increasing training volume
Risk factors that predict the development of disordered eating and eating disorders are poorly
described; however psychiatric disorders (such as depression and anxiety) and a history of
severely restrictive dieting appear to be strongly associated.

Epidemiology and Risk Factors
The Triad is most often observed in competitive athletes; however, it can affect athletes
of all skill levels. Because it is a spectrum of disease, the exact prevalence is unknown,
and estimates are wide ranging. Analysis of existing literature has shown large
discrepancies in proposed prevalence rates of any one of the Triad conditions. A
relatively small percentage (zero to 15.9%) of athletes exhibit all three components.
However, prevalence of any one of the components alone ranges from 16% to 60%
among female athletes.8
Incidence generally is higher in sports that historically place emphasis on endurance
training and/or a lean physique, such as gymnastics, swimming, dance, and distance
running.9 An increased incidence also is found in weight-classified sports, such as
wrestling and rowing.10
Certain behaviors correlate with greatest risk for low energy availability, including
limiting caloric intake; following restrictive diets, such as vegetarianism; and exercising
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:07 PM
AAOS | Female Athlete Triad
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002089
4/29

for long periods of time.6 Additional risk factors include early sport specialization and
dieting for sport. Injury and traumatic events or periods of worsened mental health are
high risk periods of time for developing restrictive behaviors. Rapidly increasing training
volume puts an athlete at risk for unintentional energy imbalance.10 Casual comments
made by coaches, parents, and friends also have been proven to have great influence on
the development of disordered eating.10 The specific risk factors that predict
development of an eating disorder remain unclear; however, a history of severely
restrictive dieting and psychiatric disorders such as depression and anxiety appear to be
the most sensitive predictors for developing a new eating disorder.11
Pathophysiology
Low Energy Availability
Energy availability is the difference between energy intake and the amount of energy
expended for exercise, daily living, and metabolic processes.
Low energy availability occurs if energy expenditure exceeds intake.
Low energy availability occurs in multiple ways: intentionally through restricted intake or
prolonged exercise, including a clinical eating disorder, or unintentionally if the athlete does
not realize energy needs are not being met.
Adequate energy availability is necessary to allow an athlete to perform to their highest level in
competition and to maintain normal physiologic functioning.
If energy availability is insufficient, the body shunts energy resources from growth and
reproduction, leading to amenorrhea, low estrogen, and a decrease in bone health.
Adequate energy availability preserves healthy reproductive function and, therefore, estrogen
production, which slows bone resorption.
Adequate energy availability also directly supports bone health by stimulating the production
of hormones that promote bone formation.
Moderately reduced energy availability can cause subclinical menstrual disturbances that may
negatively affect bone health without producing any noticeable change in menstrual cycles.

Low Energy Availability
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:07 PM
AAOS | Female Athlete Triad
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002089
5/29

Energy availability is the difference between energy intake and the amount of energy
expended by the body for exercise, daily activity, and metabolic processes. Low energy
availability occurs if energy expenditure exceeds intake. This imbalance may be
intentional through restricted intake, intentionally prolonged exercise, or a clinical eating
disorder. Some athletes also use diuretic drugs, diet pills, or laxatives to control their
weight. Low energy availability also may be unintentional if the athlete does not that
realize energy intake needs are not being met. Athletes are particularly vulnerable to
unintentionally low energy availability if changing or increasing their training regimen,
such as during the shift from high school to college athletics.12
Adequate energy availability is necessary to allow an athlete to perform to their highest
level in competition; however, adequate energy availability also is important for normal
physiologic functioning in the body. If energy availability is insufficient, the body shunts
energy resources away from growth and reproduction. This leads to amenorrhea, low
estrogen, and a decrease in bone health. Conversely, adequate energy availability
promotes bone health directly and indirectly. Adequate energy availability preserves
healthy reproductive function and, therefore, estrogen production, which curbs bone
resorption. Sufficient energy availability directly supports bone health by stimulating the
production of hormones that promote bone formation.6 Moderately reduced energy
availability may produce subclinical menstrual disturbances and subtle suppressions in
metabolic hormones, leading to stress injury, even without presence of overt
amenorrhea.13
Menstrual Dysfunction
Low energy availability leads to disruption of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) from
the hypothalamus via an unknown mechanism.
The disruption of GnRH secretion leads to a decrease in pituitary secretion of luteinizing
hormone.
The disruption of luteinizing hormone leads to subtle menstrual changes and, if allowed to
progress, may lead to oligomenorrhea and amenorrhea.
Oligomenorrhea is defined as a menstrual cycle length greater than 35 days.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:07 PM
AAOS | Female Athlete Triad
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002089
6/29

Secondary amenorrhea is defined as lack of menstruation for 3 months after being previously
well established.
Low energy availability also may cause primary amenorrhea or a delay in menarche later than
age 16 years.
Subtle menstrual changes, such as luteal phase defects and anovulation, have no symptoms
and likely go unnoticed by patients.

Menstrual Dysfunction
Low energy availability can result in a spectrum of menstrual dysfunction. Low energy
availability leads to suppression of pulsatile GnRH from the hypothalamus. The exact
mechanism of GnRH suppression by low energy availability has not yet been uncovered;
however, it likely relates to the alterations in metabolic hormones, such as insulin-like
growth factor (IGF-1), insulin, cortisol, and growth hormone, that occur with low energy
availability.6 The disruption of GnRH secretion leads to a decrease in pituitary secretion
of luteinizing hormone.14 These hormone disruptions can cause subtle changes in
menstrual function or, if severe enough, complete absence of menstruation. Changes
such as anovulation and luteal phase defects likely go unnoticed by athletes as they have
no overt symptoms. With luteal phase defects, the luteal phase is shortened, and subtle
disturbances in progesterone secretion may occur with no change in total cycle length.
Luteal phase defects may progress to anovulation; however, the athlete likely is unaware
of having anovulatory cycles because no overt symptoms are present. Oligomenorrhea
then occurs, followed by amenorrhea if energy availability is not restored.
Oligomenorrhea is defined as cycles occurring at intervals longer than 35 days.
Amenorrhea is a complete absence of menstruation for more than 3 months after
previously being well established. Low energy availability also can cause primary
amenorrhea or delay in the age of menarche after age 16 years.7
Bone Mineral Density
Low energy availability indirectly affects BMD by causing a decrease in estrogen and directly
affects BMD by decreasing bone formation.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:07 PM
AAOS | Female Athlete Triad
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002089
7/29

Low energy availability negatively affects gonadal steroids (estradiol and testosterone), IGF-1,
and other hormones that affect bone health.
Hypoestrogenism causes unfavorable bone microarchitecture and lower trabecular number.
Hypoestrogenism also affects the ability of osteocytes to respond to repetitive loading,
preventing the benefit associated with load-bearing exercise and putting athletes at risk for
stress fracture.
A stress fracture is a skeletal defect that occurs as a result of repeated stress at a level less
than the bone’s ultimate failure load but at a rate greater than the bone’s ability to repair itself.
Stress fracture may be the first presentation of the Triad, and providers must maintain a high
index of suspicion.
Athletes in impact-loading sports have bone density higher than sedentary individuals of the
same age. These benefits generally are not observed in amenorrhoeic athletes.
90% of bone mass is obtained before age 18 years. Therefore, amenorrhoeic adolescents are
at great risk of low BMD or osteoporosis in the long term if energy balance is not corrected.
A high index of suspicion and provider awareness is important to prevent not only stress
injuries that keep athletes from competing but also long-term effects on bone health during
the critical adolescent bone accrual period.

Bone Mineral Density
Low energy availability negatively affects bone health in many ways, resulting in an
increased risk of stress injury, fracture, and osteoporosis if not addressed. Energy
deficiency indirectly affects BMD by causing a decrease in estrogen and directly affects
BMD by decreasing bone formation. Growth hormone, gonadal steroids (estradiol and
testosterone), IGF-1, leptin, cortisol, triiodothyronine), dehydroepiandrosterone,
parathyroid hormone, and other hormones affect peak bone mass.15 Levels of the
aforementioned hormones are all affected by low energy availability. Estrogen deficiency
likely accounts for a smaller portion of decreased BMD than chronic undernutrition and
the resultant decrease in bone formation.16 In a randomized clinical trial of exercising
women, bone formation decreased and bone resorption increased within 5 days of
energy intake being reduced below 30 kcal/kg of fat-free mass (FFM).17 This indicates
that bone formation is highly sensitive to nutritional availability, and relatively rapid
change occurs with short-term under fueling.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:07 PM
AAOS | Female Athlete Triad
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002089
8/29

Bone strength and fracture risk depend on BMD and the internal structure and quality of
bone protein, both of which also are affected by oligomenorrhea and amenorrhea.6
Hypoestrogenism has been shown to cause unfavorable bone microarchitecture and
lower trabecular number.18 The capacity of osteocytes to respond to repetitive loading
also is impaired in low estrogen states, inducing microdamage leading to stress reaction
and eventually stress fracture.19 A stress fracture is defined as a skeletal defect that
occurs as a result of repeated stress at a level less than the bone’s ultimate failure load
but at a rate greater than the bone’s ability to repair itself. An imbalance between bone
resorption and formation occurs and results in microdamage.20 The stress fracture rate
in athletes and military recruits with menstrual dysfunction is two to four times higher
than that in individuals with normal menstrual cycles.21 Therefore, a stress fracture may
be the first sign of an underlying medical issue, including the Triad. The radiographic
appearance of a stress fracture may be delayed because of poor bone health. Advanced
imaging studies may be necessary for diagnosis.20 Therefore, a high index of suspicion is
important in athletes with risk factors for the Triad so that injuries are not missed.
Osteoporosis may be caused by bone mineral loss in adulthood and inadequate
formation of bone during childhood and adolescence. Athletes in weight-bearing sports
usually see benefit with higher BMD than age-matched nonathletes; depending on the
sport, athletes may have 5% to 30% higher BMD. More benefit is observed among those
in sports that involve impact loading, such as basketball and volleyball. Non–weight-
bearing and nonimpact sports, such as cycling and swimming, do not substantially affect
BMD;22 however, these benefits often are negated in amenorrhoeic athletes who may
have BMD similar to or lower than that of sedentary peers. Approximately 90% of peak
bone mass is attained by age 18 years, and 26% is achieved during the 2 years around
peak height velocity.23 Therefore, chronically low energy availability during the preteen
and teenage years may have substantial long-term effects on bone mass.24 It is
estimated that amenorrhoeic women lose approximately 2% to 3% of bone mass per
year if they continue untreated.25 Because these athletes are not accruing bone at the
expected rate at such a crucial time, amenorrhoeic athletes who have low BMD during
adolescence or young adulthood have a higher risk of osteoporosis and osteoporotic
fracture later in life.26,27 A high index of suspicion and provider awareness are important
to prevent not only stress injuries that keep athletes from competing but also long-term
effects on athletes’ bone health during the critical adolescent bone accrual period.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:07 PM
AAOS | Female Athlete Triad
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002089
9/29

Screening
Early detection of at-risk athletes is important for preventing progression to the clinical
endpoints of the Triad.
Triad awareness among medical providers is improving but still lacking. Many providers are
uncomfortable screening for and discussing the Triad with patients.
The preparticipation evaluation is an ideal time for screening; however, many patients present
for the first time with a stress fracture or other overuse injury.
Any stress fracture or any concern for one component of the Triad should prompt evaluation
for all the components.
The 2014 Female Athlete Triad Consensus Panel recommends 11 screening questions; positive
answers should prompt more discussion and evaluation.
Physical examination may be helpful; however, examination abnormalities are unlikely to be
observed until the disordered eating or eating disorder is severe.

Screening
Early detection of at-risk athletes is important for preventing progression to the clinical
endpoints of the Triad. Although knowledge of the Triad among physicians is improving,
many do not feel confident screening for and managing Triad conditions. A 2006 survey
revealed that 91% of clinicians, including pediatricians and gynecologists, did not feel
confident treating athletes with the Triad. Less than one-half of the providers surveyed
could name all three components of the Triad.28 Even providers with awareness and
understanding of the Triad may feel uncomfortable having a conversation with patients
or do not know how to hold this conversation. A survey of orthopaedic surgeons found
disordered eating was suspected in 59% of their female athlete patients; however, those
issues were discussed with only 31% of the patients.29
The PPE is an ideal time for screening; however, because widespread awareness of the
Triad among physicians is still lacking, appropriate screening may not occur. An at-risk
athlete may instead present to an orthopaedic office with an acute or chronic overuse
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:07 PM
AAOS | Female Athlete Triad
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002089
10/29

injury. Any stress injury in a female athlete or any concern for a component of the Triad
should prompt additional evaluation. Athletes should be screened for a history of
menstrual irregularities or amenorrhea, history of stress fractures, and recurrent
nonhealing injuries. Questions on diet, mental health, and attitude toward food are
important to ask. Athletes also should be asked about previous critical comments with
regard to eating or weight from a parent, coach, or teammate. Athletes who start sport-
specific training early, over-train, or have experienced inappropriate coaching behavior
also have a higher risk. Athletes should be questioned about their history in the sport;
the number of hours per week spent training; and the coach’s attitude toward training,
nutrition, and injury.7 The 2014 Female Athlete Triad Consensus Panel recommends the
following 11 screening questions; positive answers should prompt additional discussion
and evaluation12:
Have you ever had a menstrual period?
How old were you when you had your first menstrual period?
When was your most recent menstrual period?
How many periods have you had in the past 12 months?
Are you currently taking any female hormones (estrogen, progesterone, birth control
pills)?
Do you worry about your weight?
Are you trying to or has anyone recommended that you gain or lose weight?
Are you on a special diet or do you avoid certain types of foods or food groups?
Have you ever had an eating disorder?
Have you ever had a stress fracture?
Have you ever been told you have low BMD (osteopenia or osteoporosis)?
Physical examination may be helpful but should not be relied on to make the diagnosis
of one of the Triad components. Athletes often show no physical signs until they are
approaching the clinical endpoints of the Triad. Physical signs may include low BMI,
weight loss, bradycardia, or orthostatic hypotension. Lanugo, parotid enlargement, and
calluses on the back of the knuckles from repeatedly self-induced vomiting indicate
anorexia or bulimia.7 Any of these physical examination findings should prompt
additional evaluation for components of the Triad.

Evaluation and Diagnosis
Athletes with a history concerning for any one of the Triad components should be evaluated
for all three components.
For athletes with eating disorders or disordered eating, this evaluation should most often be
completed by an experienced multidisciplinary care team, including a physician, dietician, and
mental health professional.

Evaluation and Diagnosis
Athletes with a history concerning for any one of the Triad components should be
evaluated for all three components. After initial screening, this evaluation ideally should
be completed by an experienced multidisciplinary care team, including a physician,
dietician, and mental health professional.12 Referral to a clinic with such a team is ideal,
if available; however, these clinics are rare. If such a multidisciplinary team is not
available, then all efforts should be made to refer the athlete to a physician comfortable
in diagnosing and managing the Triad. In general, initial evaluation should include
electrolytes, chemistry, complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, thyroid
function tests, and urinalysis; however, these laboratory values may be normal, even in
chronically undernourished individuals, and normal values should not be overly
reassuring.6
Low Energy Availability
Athletes with low energy availability often have a stable weight and normal BMI.
Athletes who have been in a constant state of negative energy balance may have decreased
metabolic function that allows them to restore a steady state of energy balance and maintain
weight.
Even the best methods for identifying low energy availability are imprecise; therefore, having
at-risk athletes evaluated by a sports dietician is helpful.
Active women should aim for an intake of at least 45 kcal/kg of FFM per day to ensure enough
energy availability is available for all necessary physiologic functions.

9/3/26, 4:07 PM
AAOS | Female Athlete Triad
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002089
12/29


Low Energy Availability
Clinicians cannot diagnose low energy availability simply by evaluating for weight loss
because amenorrhoeic athletes may have a stable weight.30 Athletes who have been in a
constant state of negative energy balance may experience a decrease in metabolic
function that allows them to restore a steady state of energy balance and maintain
weight.6 Therefore, an athlete may have a stable weight and a steady energy state but
still be in a state of low energy availability. Even the best methods for identifying low
energy availability are imprecise because most methods require self-reporting of food
choices. Therefore, athletes at risk for low energy availability should be evaluated by a
registered sports dietician. Daily energy availability can be calculated as follows:
An energy availability of less than 30 kcal/kg of FFM per day has been associated with
harmful changes in bone, reproductive function, and metabolism. Active women should
aim for an intake of at least 45 kcal/kg of FFM per day to ensure enough energy is
available for all necessary physiologic functions.7 One possible marker of low energy
availability is low energy stores suggested by a BMI less than 17.5 kg/m2. BMI should not
be used in adolescents. Instead, an adolescent’s expected body weight should be
followed with a growth chart, if available. Less than 85% of expected body weight can
indicate low energy stores in adolescents; however, athletes with low energy availability
may still have a normal BMI.
Amenorrhea
Low energy availability causes FHA or hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.
The diagnosis of FHA is one of exclusion.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:07 PM
AAOS | Female Athlete Triad
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002089
13/29

The differential diagnosis for primary and secondary amenorrhea is broad and includes
endocrinopathies, hypothalamic and pituitary disorders, and hyperandrogenic disorders.
Evaluation for FHA often requires referral to an endocrinologist or specialist well versed in the
Triad.
FHA should never be inferred without additional testing to rule out other causes of menstrual
dysfunction.

Amenorrhea
In athletes and active women with primary or secondary amenorrhea, the diagnosis of
FHA is one of exclusion. Primary amenorrhea is defined as menarche after 16 years of
age in the presence of secondary sex characteristics or after 14 years of age in the
absence of secondary sex characteristics. Secondary amenorrhea occurs if a patient with
previously normal periods does not menstruate for 3 months or more. The differential
diagnosis for primary and secondary amenorrhea is broad and includes pregnancy;
endocrinopathies, such as thyroid dysfunction, primary ovarian insufficiency, and
hyperprolactinemia; and hypothalamic and pituitary disorders. Other possible causes
are hyperandrogenic conditions, including polycystic ovarian syndrome, virilizing ovarian
tumors, adrenal tumors, Cushing syndrome, and non-classic congenital adrenal
hyperplasia.7 Evaluation for these conditions often requires referral to an
endocrinologist or a specialist well versed in the Triad. Laboratory testing and,
occasionally, ovarian imaging is required based on the patient’s history and physical
examination. FHA should never be inferred without additional testing to rule out the
aforementioned conditions.
Low Bone Mass Density
Athletes with high-risk Triad features or two or more moderate-risk features should have a
dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) BMD test performed.
Adult women should have weight-bearing sites evaluated via DEXA.
For children, DEXA may be difficult to interpret because of variable bone age. Children should
have at least the posteroanterior lumbar spine and, if possible, the entire body less the head
evaluated.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:07 PM
AAOS | Female Athlete Triad
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002089
14/29

In athletes who participate in load-bearing activity, a Z-score less than -1.0 is considered lower
than expected.
In the presence of clinical risk factors (nutritional deficiency, hypoestrogenism, stress fracture),
a Z-score of -1.0 to -1.9 is considered low BMD.
DEXA should be repeated no more than every 1 to 2 years if continued risk for bone loss
exists.
Athletes who meet the following criteria should undergo DEXA BMD testing:
One or more high-risk features
History of diagnosed eating disorder
BMI of less than or equal to 17.5 kg/m2, less than 85% of estimated weight, or recent
weight loss of more than 10% in 1 month
Menarche at 16 years of age or older
Less than six menses over any 12-month period
Two prior stress reactions or fractures, one high-risk stress reaction or fracture (femoral
neck, sacrum, pelvis), or a low-energy nontraumatic fracture
Prior Z-score of less than -2
or
Two or more moderate-risk features
Current disordered eating or history of disordered eating for 6 months or more
BMI of 17.5 to 18.5 kg/m2, less than 90% estimated weight, or weight loss of 5% to 10% in 1
month
Menarche at 15 to 16 years of age
History of 6 to 8 menses over any 12-month period
One prior stress reaction or fracture
Z-score between -1 and -2
DEXA should be considered in athletes with a history of one or more non-peripheral or two
or more peripheral long bone traumatic fractures if any moderate- or high-risk features are
present. Discretion can be used based on severity of the trauma and age of the athlete at the
time of the fracture.
DEXA should be considered in athletes on medications for 6 months or more that may affect
bone health (such as oral prednisone).

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002089
15/29


Low Bone Mass Density
Adult women should have weight-bearing sites, such as the femoral neck and the
posteroanterior spine, evaluated via DEXA.6 For children, DEXA of the hip may be less
reliable because of variable skeletal development. Children and adolescents should have
at least the posteroanterior lumbar spine and, if possible, the entire body less the head
evaluated. At the hip, BMD may be normal in weight-bearing athletes, such as runners;
however, such athletes may have low BMD at the lumbar spine, which is not affected by
weight bearing.26 Because athletes participating in weight-bearing sports should have
higher BMD than sedentary age-matched controls, the ACSM recommends different
criteria than those recommended by the International Society for Clinical Densitometry.
In athletes, a Z-score less than -1.0 is considered lower than expected. In patients with
clinical risk factors (nutritional deficiency, hypoestrogenism, stress fracture), a score of
-1.0 to -1.9 is considered low BMD.6 If continued risk exists, then DEXA should be
repeated to evaluate for ongoing bone loss or assess treatment—but not any more
frequently than every 1 to 2 years.
Management
The primary goal in the management of the Triad should be restoration of energy balance.
Weight gain has been shown to reliably restore menses.
Increased energy availability can be achieved by increasing caloric intake and decreasing
energy expenditure; however, this may be difficult to accomplish in high-level athletes.
Specific targets may include reversal of recent weight loss, return to a weight associated with
normal menses, or normalization of BMI.
Weight-bearing exercise also is beneficial for BMD and should be encouraged if it can be done
safely.
Athletes with disordered eating and eating disorders should be referred to a multidisciplinary
team that includes a sports physician, psychologist, and dietitian comfortable managing these
conditions.
Improvements in menstrual function may take months; improvements in BMD may take
months to years.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:07 PM
AAOS | Female Athlete Triad
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002089
16/29

Athletes should have calcium and vitamin D levels optimized via diet and supplementation as
necessary.
Nonpharmacologic treatment options should be attempted before any pharmacologic
treatment is considered (the exception being treatment for underlying mental illness).
Oral contraceptives are not effective for normalizing menstrual function and improving BMD
and may be detrimental.
Any pharmacologic treatment, such as transdermal estrogen, should be prescribed and
managed by providers well versed in their use.

Management
Time to resumption of menses may vary and depend on the severity of the initial energy
deficit and the duration of menstrual dysfunction.31 A change in physiologic function can
occur within days of improvement of energy availability; however, improvements in
menstrual function may take months to more than 1 year.7 Occasionally, changes in
BMD may take several years and may never fully normalize, depending on the severity
and timing.36
If a patient does not respond to nonpharmacologic management, then pharmacologic
treatment options should be considered. According to the 2014 Female Athlete Triad
Consensus Statement, pharmacologic therapy may be considered in an athlete with a Z-
score of less than -2, a clinically important fracture history, or no response to 1 year of
nonpharmacologic therapy. Pharmacologic treatment also may be considered in athletes
with a Z-score between -1 and -2 who have a clinically important fracture history and two
or more additional Triad risk factors.12
The primary goal in the management of the Triad should be restoration of energy
balance. Athletes should be counseled regarding the short- and long-term effects of low
energy availability, including decreased performance and risk of injury. Weight gain has
been shown to reliably restore menses. Weight gain also has been shown to increase
BMD, indirectly by increasing estrogen levels and directly by improving energy
availability for bone formation.31 Weight gain and restoration of energy balance may be
difficult in high-level athletes with demanding training schedules. For the best likelihood

of success, treatment plans should consider the athlete’s goals and unique training
demands. Proven strategies in the literature have incorporated gradual increase in
caloric intake and decreases in training volume. The optimal amount of weight gain and
decrease in energy expenditure varies from athlete to athlete; however, an increase of
about 5% to 10% of body weight has been observed to be effective.32,33 One study
demonstrated that decreasing training volume by only one session per week in addition
to increasing caloric intake by approximately 360 k/cal per day was enough to recover
menstrual function.32 Occasionally, decreasing training volume by 1 day per week results
in the athlete training harder and longer during the other days of training.33 Specific
targets may include reversal of recent weight loss, return to a weight associated with
normal menses, or normalization of BMI to 18.5 kg/m2 or greater than 90% of predicted
weight.7 Weight gain alone has positive effects on bone health; however, resumption of
normal menstrual function likely is essential for normalization of BMD.18,34
Weight-bearing exercise also is beneficial for increasing and maintaining BMD and
should be encouraged if it can be done safely. Programs that include a combination of
high-impact loading and resistance training are effective methods for optimizing BMD;35
however, an athlete’s individual fracture risk should be considered before
recommending high-impact activity.
For athletes with low energy availability caused by inadvertent undereating, referral for
nutrition counseling (ideally by a sports dietician) usually is sufficient; however, athletes
in whom any concern for disordered eating or an eating disorder exists should be
referred to a multidisciplinary team. This team ideally includes a physician versed in the
Triad, a sports psychologist, and a sports dietitian.7 Athletes with presentations
concerning for eating disorders require substantial multidimensional care that includes
management of any concurrent anxiety, depression, or obsessive-compulsive disorder,
and occasionally includes the prescription of medications. Such athletes may be difficult
to identify because many athletes deny that a problem exists or minimize problem
behaviors. Providers must maintain a high index of suspicion and refer for additional
evaluation if concern exists.

Treatment of patients with eating disorders is complex and often combines medication,
such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, and psychotherapy. Such treatment is
best handled by a multidisciplinary team well versed in treating athletes with an eating
disorder.12 Calcium and vitamin D levels should be optimized via food intake and/or
supplementation. According to ACSM recommendations, calcium intake should optimally
be between 1,000 and 1,300 mg per day.6 Athletes who play indoor sports have an
increased risk of vitamin D deficiency. An athlete’s 25-hydroxyvitamin D level should
ideally be maintained above 50 nmol/L (20 ng/mL); however, some experts suggest levels
be maintained above 75 nmol/L (30 ng/mL).37,38 This can be accomplished via an intake
of approximately 800 IU of vitamin D per day; however, additional supplementation may
be necessary for patients who are deficient.38
Pharmacologic treatment for FHA should be reserved for athletes with evidence of low
estrogen or infertility.39 The goal should be restoration of menses and subsequent
improvement in BMD. In the past, oral contraceptives were widely used to regulate the
menstrual cycles of women with oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea; rather than being
beneficial for bone and menstrual health, this may be detrimental because of first-pass
effects on the hepatic production of IGF-1. Oral contraceptives appear to directly
suppress IGF-1 production in the liver and upregulate the synthesis of IGF-1 binding
proteins, decreasing bioavailability.40 In addition, oral contraceptives may provide a false
sense of security that the athlete’s energy status is improving by causing the athlete to
have a monthly withdrawal bleed that may be mistaken for normal menstrual function.
Recent studies have shown that transdermal estradiol may be effective for increasing
BMD in oligomenorrheic and amenorrhoeic athletes.41,42 However, transdermal
estradiol must be combined with cyclic progesterone to avoid the negative effects of
unopposed estrogen. These medications should only be prescribed by physicians well
versed with their use, such as gynecologists, endocrinologists, or physicians specializing
in the Triad. Use of transdermal estradiol should be especially considered in adolescent
and young adult athletes who should be in the process of accruing peak bone mass.
Deficits accrued during this time that are not corrected may become irreversible.43

Data on the pharmacologic management of low BMD in young athletes with the use of
traditional osteoporosis medications is lacking. An athlete’s Z-score, fracture history, and
cumulative Triad risk factors must be evaluated before pharmacologic management of
BMD is considered. Any treatment beyond estrogen replacement should not be
considered unless an athlete meets the criteria for osteoporosis, has failed
nonpharmacologic therapy with recurrent fractures, and has contraindications to
estrogen use or has not had any response after 18 to 24 months of estrogen
replacement.7 Diphosphonates have long been used for the management of
osteoporosis in postmenopausal women; however, diphosphonates have not been
studied in exercising women with the Triad. Studies in anorexic women have yielded
mixed results, with improvements in the BMD of adult women but not adolescent
women.44,45 Diphosphonates must be used with extreme caution in women of
childbearing age because they have a long half-life (up to 10 years) and are associated
with a potential for substantial teratogenic effects.26 In athletes with the Triad,
diphosphonates should only be initiated and managed by an endocrinologist or
specialist in metabolic bone diseases.7 Diphosphonates rarely should be considered in
women of childbearing age.
Return to Play
Return to play decisions for athletes with the Triad are complex and require risk stratification
of each individual athlete’s case.
The 2014 ACSM position statement provided a decision-making tool to help guide risk
stratification.
Athletes with low-risk features can be cleared for play but should continue treatment and
monitoring.
Athletes with moderate-risk features can be provisionally cleared, with the stipulation that
they continue to engage with a multidisciplinary team and work toward the goals set by the
team.
Athletes with high-risk features may be restricted from competition and training, and this
should be continually reevaluated if the athlete engages in treatment with the care team.
A written contract signed by the athlete that indicates criteria necessary for ongoing or future
clearance for play is recommended.

Return to Play
Decisions about clearance and return to play for athletes with one or more Triad
features may be difficult. Individual risk stratification is an important component of the
return to play decision. Prospective return to play data has shown that female runners
with some degree of menstrual dysfunction have more severe stress injuries observed
on MRI and a longer return to play than those with eumenorrhea.46 Athletes with low
BMD also are more prone to stress fractures in areas of trabecular bone, such as the
femoral neck and pelvis, which generally have longer recovery time.47 Therefore, risk
stratification is important for injury prevention and safe return to play for athletes with
one or more of the Triad syndromes. The 2014 ACSM position statement provides
guidance for clinicians in a the form of a decision-making tool (Figures 1 and 2).

Athletes who are low risk can be cleared for return to play if they have no other medical
condition that would disqualify them. Referral to a multidisciplinary team is not
mandatory for low-risk athletes, and the decision to refer is based on the individual
athlete and provider comfort. Moderate-risk athletes can be provisionally cleared or
cleared in a limited capacity for return to play. Clearance for these athletes is contingent
on continuing to engage in care with a multidisciplinary team and comply with the care
team’s recommendations. Specific limitations on training load, frequency, and intensity
may be set by the care team and may be altered if the athlete’s health status changes.
Athletes who are high risk may be restricted from competition and training. A plan
should be outlined for the athlete, and clearance should be reevaluated if the athlete’s
health status improves. A written contract signed by the athlete that indicates criteria
necessary for ongoing or future clearance for play is recommended. Contracts facilitate a
clear and shared understanding between the athlete and the parties involved with their
care. Clearance for moderate- and high-risk athletes is complex and must be
individualized to each athlete. Therefore, clearance should be determined and managed
by teams familiar with diagnosis and management of the Triad. Consideration must be
given to not only the athlete’s physiologic risk but also the risk inherent in the sport and
the athlete’s willingness to engage in treatment with the team.7

Providers must maintain a high index of suspicion for the components of the Triad in
evaluating physically active girls and women.
Diagnosis early in the disease course may prevent progression to the clinical endpoints of
disordered eating, osteoporosis, and amenorrhea.
Ideally, screening should take place during the preparticipation examination but also should
occur if the athlete presents with a stress injury or any other findings concerning for the Triad.

a sports physician, psychologist, and nutritionist.
Management should be aimed at restoring energy balance via increased caloric intake and
decreased training volume.

Conclusion
In evaluating physically active girls and women, especially athletes participating in high-
risk sports, providers must maintain a high index of suspicion for the components of the
Triad. The three components are low energy availability with or without disordered
eating, menstrual dysfunction, and low BMD. Diagnosis early in the disease course may
prevent progression to the clinical endpoints of disordered eating, osteoporosis, and
amenorrhea. Ideally, screening should take place during preparticipation examination
but also should occur if an athlete presents with a stress injury or other findings
concerning for a component of the Triad. For the best chance of success, evaluation and
management should take place with a multidisciplinary team that can address the
physical, psychologic, and nutritional factors. Management should be primarily focused
on restoring energy balance via increased caloric intake or potentially decreased training
volume. Early detection and successful management prevents long-term struggles with
menstrual dysfunction and low BMD and allows athletes to continue to compete
recreationally or at the highest level.
